title: H-1B Visa Filings Surge in Texas Even as Republican Leaders Crack Down
excerpt: Private-sector demand for H-1B workers in Texas remains strong despite Governor Abbott's freeze on state hiring and growing MAGA backlash against the visa program.
body:
• Private-sector H-1B filings in Texas continue to climb even as Governor Greg Abbott has frozen state and university petitions through May 2027
  • Texas ranks second only to California in total H-1B approvals, with Cognizant, Oracle, and Tesla among the state's top sponsors
  • Attorney General Ken Paxton has launched probes into alleged H-1B "ghost offices" in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, fueling local MAGA backlash
  • Indians make up an estimated 71% of all approved H-1B applications nationally, making them the community most exposed to the shifting policy landscape

Texas has become the central battleground in America's fight over the H-1B visa program. Even as Republican state leaders have launched an aggressive crackdown on the skilled-worker visa, private-sector filings in the state continue to surge, underscoring the deep reliance of Texas's booming tech and energy economy on foreign talent.

Abbott's Freeze and the Public-Sector Fallout

In January 2026, Governor Greg Abbott ordered all state agencies and public universities to immediately halt new H-1B visa petitions. The freeze, which runs through May 31, 2027, requires institutions to obtain written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission before filing any new petitions.

"State government must lead by example and ensure that employment opportunities — particularly those funded with taxpayer dollars — are filled by Texans first."

— Greg Abbott, Governor of Texas

The directive has sent ripples through Texas's public university system. Major research institutions including UT Southwestern Medical Center and MD Anderson Cancer Center, which together employ hundreds of H-1B visa holders, face disrupted hiring pipelines. Over the past six years, Texas hospitals alone have sponsored more than 500 doctoral students through the program.

Immigration attorney Faye Kolly, founding partner of Austin-based McChesney Kolly, warned of broader consequences. "Our best state institutions, universities, will have trouble recruiting people, because they can just go elsewhere. They can go to 49 other states, or outside of the U.S.," she said.

Private Sector Tells a Different Story

While state entities account for only about 5% of the top 25 Texas H-1B employers, the private sector continues to file aggressively. Cognizant Technology Solutions leads with more than 3,100 approved visas in the state, followed by Oracle, Tesla, and several major Indian IT firms including TCS, Infosys, and Wipro, all of which have large Texas operations.

The demand reflects Texas's emergence as a tech hub rivaling California, with companies relocating headquarters and expanding operations across Austin, Dallas, and Houston. Abbott's freeze does not affect private-sector companies, creating a two-tier system where corporate employers continue hiring while public institutions are locked out.

MAGA Backlash and "Ghost Office" Probes

The crackdown extends beyond the governor's office. Attorney General Ken Paxton has issued civil investigative demands to employers suspected of operating H-1B "ghost offices" — fraudulent businesses sponsoring high numbers of visa applicants with little actual commercial activity. Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows has also directed a legislative committee to investigate employer use of the program.

The tensions have spilled into public life. At a Frisco City Council meeting, attendees accused H-1B workers of an "Indian takeover" of local communities, though Indian-American residents and local leaders pushed back, citing the community's economic and cultural contributions.

The Federal Landscape

Texas's state-level actions come on top of federal changes that have reshaped the H-1B landscape. President Trump's September 2025 proclamation imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, and the Department of Homeland Security restructured the lottery to prioritize higher-wage petitions. Congress is also considering the bipartisan H-1B and L-1 Visa Reform Act of 2025, which would establish stricter wage baselines.

What This Means for Indian Workers

With Indians accounting for approximately 71% of all approved H-1B applications, the community is disproportionately affected by every shift in the policy landscape. Texas is home to thousands of Indian tech professionals concentrated in the Dallas-Fort Worth corridor and Houston metro, many of whom now face a complex web of state restrictions, federal fee hikes, and mounting public hostility — even as their employers continue to rely on them to fill roles that cannot be sourced domestically.

The contradiction at the heart of Texas's H-1B story is clear: the same state that is cracking down on the visa program with one hand continues to depend on it with the other.
